strengths: Integrating label propagation and label spreading into density-ratio-based Bayesian optimization is a plausible, practically motivated contribution. The framework handles both generated unlabeled points and existing candidate pools, and its relationship to BORE and LFBO is clearly acknowledged.

The empirical evaluation covers synthetic functions, tabular hyperparameter optimization, NATS-Bench, and an image-based search task, with ten runs per setting. Comparisons include GP-EI/UCB and multiple classifier implementations of BORE/LFBO. The reported gains, particularly on NATS-Bench, are promising.

The supplementary experiments investigate kernel bandwidth, unlabeled-point counts, sampling distributions, and pool subsampling. The comparison with no unlabeled data provides some evidence that propagation contributes beyond the underlying kernel predictor.
weaknesses: The sampling strategy does not establish the cluster assumption on which the theoretical motivation depends. Sampling truncated Gaussians around evaluated points cannot ensure that high-density regions share the objective-derived label: components centered on nearby observations with opposite labels can overlap. In the continuous setting, these generated points supply a chosen geometric prior, rather than independent evidence that the unknown objective respects that geometry.

Section 4.3 does not establish the claimed advantage for the proposed algorithm. Equations (11)–(13) invoke an existence result for semi-supervised classification, without showing that label propagation or label spreading attains the bound. Applicability to adaptively collected observations and changing quantile labels is also unestablished. Moreover, lower classification risk does not directly imply better acquisition maximizers or optimization regret. The assertion following Equation (8) that this predictor is better than or equivalent to supervised alternatives therefore exceeds the evidence.

The central explanation concerning overconfidence remains largely qualitative. Section 3.1 defines it as concentration of high class probabilities, but the paper provides no quantitative measure connecting that concentration to exploration or optimization performance. The no-unlabeled-data ablation covers only two synthetic functions. Comparisons controlling for kernel bandwidth and the random tie-breaking heuristic, including an exploration-enhanced BORE baseline, would help determine what actually causes the gains.

Important experimental details remain unspecified: the main experiments' kernel-bandwidth selection, clamping factor, feature scaling and categorical encoding, and candidate selection within discrete pools despite the stated use of L-BFGS-B. These omissions matter because the bandwidth ablation shows substantial sensitivity. The shaded uncertainty bands are also undefined, and runtime or memory measurements are absent despite dense graph construction and 1,000 optimization restarts. Together, these gaps limit reproducibility and assessment of practical performance.

The MNIST experiment uses embeddings from a network trained on 440,000 examples labeled with the same three-digit target being optimized (Section S.3.4). Although all optimizers share this representation, the experiment consequently assumes substantial prior objective supervision. Directly ranking candidates using that pretrained classifier is an important missing baseline for establishing the value of the sequential optimization procedure.

A smaller but relevant mathematical presentation issue occurs in Section 4.1: the stated column-normalized definition of p_ij corresponds to W D^{-1}, whereas the text gives P = D^{-1}W and Equation (6) uses P transposed. The normalization and propagation conventions should be made consistent so the intended implementation is unambiguous.
